title: Brand identity when you only have a name
metaTitle: Startup brand identity, starting from a name
excerpt: A startup brand can begin with a name if you settle the audience, the offer, and the feeling you refuse. Type, color, and one sentence do the rest.
alt: Blue and orange ink blooming through water. The frame is color arriving before any mark, which is the right order when a company still only has a name.
caption: Color before a mark. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Can we launch a site before the logo is finished?
faqs.answer: Yes, if the audience, the offer, and the sentence are settled and the type and colors are already chosen. A temporary wordmark in the text face is enough for a first page. Commission the final mark when those decisions are stable, and replace the wordmark without changing the sentence.

faqs.question: How many references should a young brand collect?
faqs.answer: Three that survive the refusal you wrote down. A folder of thirty images feels like research and usually hides a disagreement. If you cannot say why a reference stays, it does not belong in the set.

faqs.question: What if we only have a domain and a rough offer?
faqs.answer: Write the offer in one sentence a buyer could repeat, and name the feeling you refuse. The domain can wait if the word is still unstable. Branding a name you expect to change produces files you will throw away.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A startup brand identity can start from a name if you settle three decisions before anyone draws a mark: who it is for, what you offer them, and the feeling you refuse. The name is the seed. The system is a typeface, a short color list, and one sentence the site can repeat.

That sentence is on a clock. [Nielsen Norman Group](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) found that people often leave a page within 10 to 20 seconds, and that a clear value proposition within 10 seconds is what earns a longer stay. A poetic name can sit in the corner. The line under it has to say what this is. [Google's guidance on helpful content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks a related question of the whole site: whether it has a primary purpose. A brand that tries to sound like every category at once fails that test on its own homepage.

## Audience, offer, and the feeling you refuse

Write the audience as a person with a job. "Founders preparing a first conversation with customers" is a brief. "Anyone who cares about quality" is a wish. If you cannot picture the person who will read the homepage, color choices will drift toward whatever the designer likes that week.

Write the offer as the thing they can start this month. A studio that designs and builds a website is a different company from a studio that only advises. A shop that sells one object is a different company from a catalog of everything. The offer keeps the identity attached to a transaction, a conversation, or a product someone can open.

Then write the feeling you refuse. This filter does more work than a moodboard. A heritage craft brand may refuse gloss and hurry. A community sports club may refuse the tone of a private club. A software tool may refuse the look of a toy. When a reference fails the refusal, it leaves the set. You do not need twenty references. You need three that survive the filter, and a sentence that explains why.

Put the three lines on one page. Audience. Offer. Refusal. That page is the brief. Type, color, and a logo come after it, and they have to answer to it.

## What the name is allowed to carry

A name has to be sayable, spellable, and possible to type. It can be a container. It can pick up meaning from the sentence beside it. It does the least harm when it stays true if the product grows by one step.

Say it out loud in the sentence a stranger would repeat: the name, then who it helps, then the offer. If the name and the sentence fight, the sentence is still vague, or the name is trying to be a paragraph. Fix the sentence. Names get expensive to change once they are on a bank account, a domain, and a contract.

Do a practical collision check before you fall in love with the word. Can you use a domain you can actually own? Can you claim a handle a buyer would guess? Does the word mean something you would not want in the language your buyers use? This is a filter for the week you are choosing, and a lawyer still has to speak to trademark. The filter stops you from briefing a whole identity around a word you cannot ship.

Leave a little emptiness in the name. A word that describes only the first feature will feel wrong when the second feature is the one customers mention. The company name should still fit if the offer widens. Product names, which have to sit in a URL and a sentence of their own, are a separate decision with a harder future test.

## Type, color, and the sentence the site repeats

Choose one typeface for headlines and one for running text, or one family with two clear roles. Read them at the size of a phone headline and at the size of a paragraph in a dim room. If a third face is required for "personality," the personality is still unresolved. A pair is enough for a homepage, a deck, and an invoice.

Keep the color list short: a background, a text color, one accent, and one quiet support color. Name them by use. "Accent" is an instruction. A poetic color name, sitting alone, invites the next person to pick a cousin of that color and call it close enough. You can keep a human nickname if the use name is printed beside it.

Write the sentence the site will repeat. It answers what this is and what a visitor can do next. A quiet brand line can stay if the following sentence is plain. On Hanabi's own site the brand line is short, and the plainer line says the studio designs and builds websites and product interfaces for founders. The pattern is the lesson: the name carries tone, and the next sentence carries the offer.

The first screen has room for that pair and one action. A manifesto, a timeline, and a grid of values can wait until someone has asked for them. Nielsen's finding is a writing constraint, not a slogan about speed. If the value is missing from the first view, the rest of the page is a reward for people who already decided to stay.

## What to postpone until the sentence exists

Postpone a mascot, a pattern language, an illustration world, and a motion study. They are easy to admire and hard to apply to a button, a favicon, and a receipt in the same month. They also freeze taste before the offer is stable.

Postpone the long guidelines book. A team that can still meet in one room will not maintain forty pages, and they will not open them on a Thursday afternoon. The useful deliverable, while you only have a name, is the brief, the type pair, the color list, the sentence, and files a developer can drop into a page.

If a mark already exists, from a friend or a generator, hold it lightly. A charming drawing that fails at the size of a browser tab will tax every layout you ship. The tests for that drawing come next: small, on a dark surface, and beside type. Until it passes, build the page around the sentence.

## How the first page should use the work

The homepage is the first place the system either holds or frays. Set the sentence in the type you chose. Use the background and the text color as specified. Let the accent appear on the action, and almost nowhere else. A visitor should feel one material, one voice, and one next step.

Proof can be quiet and still be proof. Name a project, show the work, or describe who you have already helped in plain words. A young company that states its offer looks more credible than a young company that borrows the voice of a larger one. Skip invented numbers. Skip awards you do not have. A single true paragraph about a real engagement beats a row of empty badges.

Read the page with the logo covered. The sentence should still tell a stranger where they are. Read it with the sentence covered. The logo will usually go quiet, and that is acceptable this early. If the sentence also goes quiet, the identity is still only a name, and the page is decorating a gap.

## When to bring in a studio

Bring in help when the decisions are made and the making is the bottleneck. That moment looks like this: the audience and the offer are written, the refusal is real, and you need a mark, a site, and a handoff your team can edit without inventing a second palette. [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services) cover identity and the site in one engagement when those should be the same project.

Wait if the name is still a maybe. Branding a maybe produces files you will resent. Settle the three lines, then put the mark through its tests. The next piece, [A logo is not a brand system](/blog/logo-and-the-system-around-it), is about those tests, and about what has to exist around the mark so the second page stays in the same family.
